summary:
TERRANOVA is a project created by our group (PSB ASTRO MINDS). It allows you to explore 10 different locations on earth that would be useful to test equipment, tech and experimenting for Moon and Mars missions.

It was thought that if we were going to send something to another planet, why not test it somewhere on earth with similar conditions.

We used NASA images, environmental data, lunar topography maps, historical data and research to find locations that had similar features. We looked at many factors including topography, minerals, permafrost and what difficulties may be involved.

For example we found that Omongwa (Namibia) contains some gypsum which means it is a very interesting place to test techniques we can use on Mars. However some comparisons aren’t perfect. For example Kula has very steep volcanic terrain compared to the lunar area it was being compared to.

This was something we wanted to highlight in TERRANOVA. The Earth is not the Moon or Mars so we cannot recreate all conditions.

We have tried to make this information easy to explore. There are suggestions on what experiments you could do, evidence to back up why the location is useful, research sources and any key limitations.

We hope this will help students, researchers and robotic teams find some great locations to test in the future whilst understanding why the location is useful.
details:
TERRANOVA

It is an interactive web application created by PSB ASTRO MINDS aiming to link locations on Earth to proposed experiments for missions to the Moon and Mars. It considers why certain locations are useful for a specific experiment.

How it works:

The user can explore an in-depth 3D map of Earth, toggle between Moon and Mars, and select one of ten researched locations. Upon selecting a location the user will be zoomed in to the location. They will be shown pictures, a mission proposal, evidence for the experiment and any limitations to the location. Information is shown gradually.

Research has been done using NASA GIBS images, NASA POWER environmental data, LRO/LOLA topographic data, observations from the planetary archive, free topographic data of Earth and scientific studies. For five locations on the Moon, slope and relief were calculated for a consistent scale. For Mars, specific links were explored such as mineralogy, sample handling and drilling. The application shows what has been calculated by the team, observed in publications and what experiments have been proposed.

Observations from publications show gypsum has been found at Omongwa, Namibia and Olympia Undae on Mars which supports our proposed rover experiment to search for minerals. Kula, Türkiye had much steeper relief than the chosen lunar location from our measurements. This means it does not have similar relief but could be a good location for practicing difficult rover situations.

Benefits and Impact:

TERRANOVA could support researchers, robotics teams, universities and students to identify suitable environments on Earth. It provides clarity with the mission, evidence and limitations. This aims to provide more knowledge when preparing for exploration using focused experiments on Earth. Next steps would involve surveying an exact testing area and trialling equipment. We have not yet tested how well the equipment would work in the field or what cost savings there would be.

Technology & Creativity:

This application was created using React, Typescript, CesiumJS and Vite. Python scripts were used to help with the research analysis. The application is hosted on Vercel. The user can look at a globe, location pictures, comparison visuals and animations showing examples of the mission.

Each location has been linked to a specific task. Why the analogy works or does not work has been explained. Geology, mineralogy, slope, terrain obstacles, permafrost, local weather, solar power, sampling, power and drilling were considered depending on what experiment was proposed.

This is a selection of researched locations, they may not be suitable facilities in the field or guarantee new discoveries for NASA. Gravity, vacuum and thin atmosphere cannot be replicated on Earth. These limitations have been recognised in our scientific reasoning.
